section.title: The Healing of Naaman
section.sectionRationale: A powerful Aramean commander with leprosy is directed by a captured Israelite girl toward Elisha, and after resisting the prophet's humble prescription, washes in the Jordan and is healed, confessing the LORD as the only true God. The chapter closes with Elisha's servant Gehazi secretly seizing payment Elisha refused, and inheriting Naaman's leprosy as judgment.
section.thesis: The LORD freely heals and saves a pagan foreigner who humbles himself to obey a simple word, while His own servant, grasping for gain, receives the very disease grace had just removed, showing that the LORD's blessing is received by humble faith, not achieved by status or seized by greed.
section.frameNote: Four beats: Naaman's condition and the servant girl's word, verses 1 to 7; Elisha's prescription and Naaman's initial rage, verses 8 to 14; Naaman's confession and Elisha's refusal of payment, verses 15 to 19; and Gehazi's greed and resulting leprosy, verses 20 to 27.

units.label: Naaman's condition and the servant girl's word
units.note: there is a prophet in Samaria

verses.text: Now Naaman, the commander of the army of the king of Aram, was a great man in his master's sight and highly regarded, for through him the LORD had given victory to Aram. And he was a mighty man of valor, but he was a leper.
At this time the Arameans had gone out in bands and had taken a young girl from the land of Israel, and she was serving Naaman's wife.
She said to her mistress, "If only my master would go to the prophet who is in Samaria, he would cure him of his {{tsaraath|leprosy}}."
And Naaman went and told his master what the girl from the land of Israel had said.

"Go now," said the king of Aram, "and I will send you with a letter to the king of Israel." So Naaman departed, taking with him ten talents of silver, six thousand shekels of gold, and ten sets of clothing.
And the letter that he took to the king of Israel stated: "With this letter I am sending my servant Naaman, so that you may cure him of his leprosy."

When the king of Israel read the letter, he tore his clothes and asked, "Am I God, killing and giving life, that this man expects me to cure a leper? Surely you can see that he is seeking a quarrel with me!"

Now when Elisha the man of God heard that the king of Israel had torn his clothes, he sent a message to the king: "Why have you torn your clothes? Please let the man come to me, and he will know that there is a prophet in Israel."
So Naaman came with his horses and chariots and stood at the door of Elisha's house.
Then Elisha sent him a messenger, who said, "Go and wash yourself seven times in the Jordan, and your flesh will be restored, and you will be clean."
But Naaman went away angry, saying, "I thought that he would surely come out, stand and call on the name of the LORD his God, and wave his hand over the spot to cure my leprosy.
Are not the Abanah and Pharpar, the rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of Israel? Could I not have washed in them and been cleansed?" So he turned and went away in a rage.

Naaman's servants, however, approached him and said, "My father, if the prophet had told you to do some great thing, would you not have done it? How much more, then, when he tells you, 'Wash and be cleansed'?"
So Naaman went down and dipped himself in the Jordan seven times, according to the word of the man of God, and his flesh was restored and became like that of a little child, and he was clean.

units.label: Naaman's confession and Elisha's refusal
units.note: there is no God in all the earth except in Israel

verses.text: Then Naaman and all his attendants went back to the man of God, stood before him, and declared, "Now I know for sure that there is no God in all the earth except in Israel. So please accept a gift from your servant."
But Elisha replied, "As surely as the LORD lives, before whom I stand, I will not accept it." And although Naaman urged him to accept it, he refused.

"If you will not," said Naaman, "please let me, your {{eved|servant}}, be given as much {{adamah|soil}} as a pair of mules can carry. For your servant will never again make a burnt offering or a sacrifice to any other god but the LORD.

Yet may the LORD forgive your servant this one thing: When my master goes into the temple of Rimmon to worship there, and he leans on my arm, and I bow down in the temple of Rimmon, may the LORD forgive your servant in this matter."
"Go in {{shalom|peace}}," said Elisha. But after Naaman had traveled a short distance,

units.label: Gehazi's greed and leprosy
units.note: the leprosy of Naaman will cling to you

verses.text: Gehazi, the servant of Elisha the man of God, said, "Look, my master has spared this Aramean, Naaman, by not accepting what he brought. As surely as the LORD lives, I will run after him and get something from him."
So Gehazi pursued Naaman. And when Naaman saw him running toward him, he got down from the chariot to meet him and asked, "Is everything all right?"

"Everything is all right," Gehazi replied. "My master has sent me to say, 'Look, two young men from the sons of the prophets have just now come to me from the hill country of Ephraim. Please give them a talent of silver and two sets of clothing.'"

But Naaman insisted, "Please, take two talents." And he urged Gehazi to accept them. Then he tied up two talents of silver in two bags along with two sets of clothing and gave them to two of his servants, who carried them ahead of Gehazi.
When Gehazi came to the hill, he took the gifts from the servants and stored them in the house. Then he dismissed the men, and they departed.
When Gehazi went in and stood before his master, Elisha asked him, "Gehazi, where have you been?" "Your servant did not go anywhere," he replied.

But Elisha questioned him, "Did not my spirit go with you when the man got down from his chariot to meet you? Is this the time to accept money and clothing, olive groves and vineyards, sheep and oxen, menservants and maidservants?
Therefore, the leprosy of Naaman will cling to you and your descendants forever!" And as Gehazi left his presence, he was leprous, as white as snow.

tsaraath.gloss: A term for various skin diseases translated leprosy, treated at length in Leviticus 13 to 14 as ritually defiling. It afflicts a celebrated pagan general and, by the chapter's end, Elisha's own greedy servant, showing that no rank exempts anyone from needing the LORD's cleansing.

adamah.gloss: Soil, earth, or ground. Naaman's request for Israelite soil reflects an ancient belief that a god was tied to his land; taking earth home was likely meant to let him worship the LORD on His own ground even while living in Aram, an early, imperfect step of a genuine new faith.

shalom.gloss: Peace, wholeness, or well being. Elisha's parting words to Naaman, go in shalom, release the healed foreigner in blessing despite the moral complexity of his continuing court duties, entrusting him fully to the LORD's mercy rather than imposing a rigid demand.

eved.gloss: Servant or slave. Naaman repeatedly calls himself Elisha's eved after his healing, a striking reversal for a powerful commander, and the same word Gehazi twice denies being sent as, your servant did not go anywhere, exposing his lie even as he claims the title honestly belongs to him under Elisha.

basic.context: Naaman, a celebrated Aramean general, has leprosy, and a young Israelite captive girl points him toward Elisha. The king of Israel panics at the request to heal him, but Elisha calls Naaman to himself. Offended that Elisha does not personally perform a dramatic ritual, Naaman nearly leaves in anger, but his own servants persuade him to try the simple instruction: wash seven times in the Jordan. He is healed, confesses the LORD as the only true God, and offers payment, which Elisha refuses. Naaman asks to take Israelite soil home and pre-emptively asks pardon for a compromise he foresees. Elisha's servant Gehazi, however, secretly chases Naaman down, lies to obtain payment, lies again to Elisha, and receives Naaman's leprosy as judgment.
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative describing a specific miraculous healing and its aftermath; it is not a proof that ritual washing itself heals disease, nor a general policy on compromise in worship. What endures is that God's grace reaches beyond Israel to a Gentile who humbles himself in simple obedience, and that grasping for what God has freely given, rather than trusting Him, brings serious consequences.
basic.originalLanguages: Naaman suffers tsaraath, a skin affliction rendered leprosy, the very disease that later falls on Elisha's own servant. His request for Israelite adamah, soil, reflects the ancient assumption that a god was bound to a particular land, an imperfect but genuine step of new faith. Elisha's dismissal, go in shalom, releases Naaman in peace despite unresolved moral tension, while Gehazi's repeated claim to be no one's eved, servant, when questioned, unmasks the very lie that costs him everything.
basic.typology: Naaman's cleansing through simple, humble obedience to a word rather than an impressive ritual anticipates the pattern of salvation by faith rather than by human achievement or status, while Gehazi's grasping after what grace had freely refused warns against turning God's gifts into personal gain.
basic.christ: Naaman's healing, received only when he humbled himself to obey a simple word rather than demand a dramatic display fitting his rank, pictures how salvation comes not to the impressive but to the humble who simply trust and obey what Christ says, as Paul later reasons that the gospel confounds the proud and saves through what seems foolish to the world, 1 Corinthians 1:26-29. Naaman, a Gentile outsider, is cleansed while many lepers in Israel were not, a truth Jesus Himself cites in Luke 4:27 to explain why God's grace was never confined to ethnic Israel alone.
basic.god: God is free to extend His saving mercy to a foreign enemy general, showing His grace is not confined to Israel by birth but reaches all who humble themselves before Him. He is also holy and cannot be used for personal profit; Elisha's refusal of payment protects the truth that God's grace is free, and Gehazi's judgment shows that greed dressed in religious service still meets real consequences.
basic.crossReferences: Luke 4:27 has Jesus cite Naaman's healing to explain God's grace reaching beyond Israel's own borders even in the Old Testament. Leviticus 14 provides the background ritual law for skin disease that this account presupposes and, in a sense, bypasses through simple obedient faith. Acts 8:18-24 tells of Simon trying to buy the gift of the Spirit, a parallel warning against treating God's grace as a commodity.
basic.oneStory: A proud Gentile commander is healed and brought to confess the LORD alone as God through humble obedience, while a grasping insider forfeits blessing through greed, together previewing the gospel pattern: God's grace reaches the humble outsider by faith, while those who try to seize or commercialize what is freely given find only judgment.

context.literary:
The chapter is framed by a single disease travelling from one end of the story to the other. It opens naming Naaman a mighty man of valor, but he was a leper, verse 1, and it closes with Gehazi leaving Elisha's presence leprous, as white as snow, verse 27. That inclusio turns the whole account into a study in reversal, the celebrated outsider is cleansed and the trusted insider is struck, so that by the final verse the reader's sympathy has moved entirely from where it started.

Pairs and doublings structure the middle of the story. Naaman brings two kinds of currency, silver and gold, and two kinds of goods, garments and metal, verse 5. After his healing he makes two requests of Elisha, soil and pardon, verses 17 to 18. Gehazi in turn tells two lies, one to Naaman about the young men from Ephraim, verse 22, and one to Elisha about never having gone anywhere, verse 25, and the second lie is the one that exposes him, since Elisha's question, did not my spirit go with you, shows he already knows the answer before Gehazi speaks.

The geography also traces a deliberate arc, from Aram to Israel's king, from the king to Elisha's house, from Elisha's house down to the Jordan and back up again, then from Israel out toward Aram once more before the narrative doubles back a final time as Gehazi runs after the very man who has just left. Every major turn in the plot happens at a threshold, a door, a river, a chariot, marking this as a story about who is let in and who is sent away.
context.historical:
The sums of Naaman's cargo, ten talents of silver and six thousand shekels of gold, come to roughly seven hundred and fifty pounds of silver and a hundred and fifty pounds of gold by the BSB's own conversion, an almost absurd fortune for what Elisha in the end refuses to touch at all, underscoring how little the healing had to do with Naaman's ability to pay for it. A royal letter of introduction, verse 6, was standard diplomatic protocol for a foreign dignitary travelling on state business, which is exactly why the king of Israel panics, he assumes a political trap rather than recognising a prophet's authority operating entirely outside his own control.

The officer on whose arm the king leaned, verse 18, held a real and known court office, a personal attendant close enough to physically support his king during public ceremony, which explains why Naaman's continuing service would require him to be physically present, bowing as his master bowed, inside the temple of Rimmon, the storm god Hadad worshipped at Damascus under that title. Captured foreign girls serving in the households of enemy officers, as the Israelite girl does for Naaman's wife, were an ordinary consequence of the border raiding that filled these decades of Aramean and Israelite conflict.

Skin disease under Israelite law, Leviticus 13, carried social consequences far beyond physical discomfort, exclusion from the community and its worship until a priest pronounced a person clean again. That an Aramean commander's affliction is even called tsaraath, the same term Israel's own law used, signals that the narrator is deliberately placing a foreigner inside categories usually reserved for describing Israel's own ritual life.
context.canonical:
Israel already had its own precedents for this disease striking the proud. Miriam is struck leprous, white as snow, for challenging Moses' unique authority, Numbers 12:10, and centuries later King Uzziah is struck with leprosy on his forehead the moment he grows arrogant enough to usurp the priesthood, 2 Chronicles 26:19, living isolated and cut off from the house of the LORD until his death. Against that backdrop it is striking that in this chapter leprosy first belongs to a foreign general who is healed, and only falls on an Israelite, Elisha's own servant, at the very end, an inversion of the pattern readers would expect.

The chapter becomes one of the clearest Old Testament arguments that the LORD's mercy was never fenced inside Israel's own borders. Jesus makes this reading explicit and provocative, reminding his hometown synagogue that there were many lepers in Israel in the time of Elisha the prophet, yet not one of them was cleansed, only Naaman the Syrian, Luke 4:27, a comment that so enrages his hearers they try to throw him off a cliff, Luke 4:28-29.

Later still, when Jesus heals ten lepers on the road to Jerusalem, Luke 17:11-19, the one who returns to give thanks is again a foreigner, a Samaritan, while nine Israelites receive the same mercy and walk away without a word, the pattern of this chapter repeating itself almost exactly six centuries later.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The author places this account inside a book largely concerned with proving to Israel that there is a prophet in Israel, verse 8, whose word can be trusted even when kings cannot be. The immediate point is polemical, an enemy nation, indeed an enemy commander who has personally brought Aram victory over Israel, verse 1, is forced by his own affliction to discover what Israel's own frightened king does not act on, that the LORD's prophet holds real power his king does not.

But the chapter's deeper aim cuts toward Israel itself rather than away from it. A captured Israelite slave girl speaks with more simple faith than the king of Israel, who tears his clothes in despair, verse 7, and a foreign general ends the story more faithful, confessing there is no God in all the earth except in Israel, than Elisha's own household servant, who ends it diseased for greed. The original audience, living inside a covenant community that regularly failed to trust the LORD as this outsider does, was meant to feel the rebuke as much as the encouragement, privilege of birth is no substitute for humble obedience, and its absence is no barrier to it.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
This is a single historical healing and its aftermath, not a manual for treating skin disease or a universal rule about how converts must handle inherited social obligations. Washing seven times in a specific river on a specific day describes what obedience looked like for Naaman, it is not a ritual formula for readers to repeat, and Elisha's refusal of payment describes his own conviction about this particular gift of grace, not a rule that ministers must never receive support for their work, compare 1 Corinthians 9:14.

The chapter also resists being read as settling every question of Christian conduct in a compromised culture. Naaman's request for pardon regarding the temple of Rimmon describes a real, unresolved tension for a very new believer still bound by state duty, and Elisha's brief answer, go in peace, neither commands every convert to remain in a similar position nor condemns Naaman for asking honestly about it. What endures is the pattern underneath the details, humility that obeys a simple word instead of demanding an impressive one, and honesty that brings unresolved struggles to God rather than hiding them.

debates.question: Did Elisha's answer, go in peace, verse 19, approve Naaman's anticipated continued attendance at the temple of Rimmon?

views.label: A pastoral accommodation for a young, imperfect convert
views.case: Naaman has just come to genuine faith and remains bound by state duty to physically assist his king in a pagan temple. Elisha's blessing, offered without further rebuke, may reflect wise patience with a new believer still working out what exclusive worship of the LORD requires inside a pagan court he cannot simply leave.

views.label: A customary farewell that leaves the ethical question deliberately open
views.case: Elisha's brief reply may be simply the ordinary courtesy of a formal goodbye rather than a considered verdict, so that the text refuses to resolve, one way or the other, exactly how far a convert may go in outward participation in a surrounding pagan structure he cannot fully escape.

debates.bearing: Either way the text does not present Naaman's situation as a pattern to copy without thought, but it shows God's grace meeting a genuine, still developing convert with patience rather than an immediate demand for perfect separation he is not yet able to make.

debates.question: Does the leprosy will cling to you and your descendants forever, verse 27, describe a literal hereditary curse?

views.label: A real, transmitted disease carried by Gehazi's line
views.case: The wording matches other Old Testament curse formulas that bind consequences to a family line, compare the sword that will never depart from David's house, 2 Samuel 12:10, so the most natural reading takes forever and descendants at face value, an actual disease passed down as long as that line continued.

views.label: Covenant lawsuit language for total and lasting disgrace
views.case: Ancient Near Eastern treaty curses regularly use family language and forever to express complete, irreversible shame rather than a strict biological guarantee, so the sentence may function chiefly to mark Gehazi's public and permanent disqualification from honourable service rather than to predict every future descendant's health.

debates.bearing: Both readings agree that Elisha's sentence transfers, exactly and visibly, the very affliction grace had just removed from Naaman onto the servant who tried to sell what God had given away freely, making greed dressed as ministry the one thing this chapter treats as more dangerous than being a leper in the first place.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 1 introduces Naaman with a jarring Hebrew construction, ish gadol, a great man, immediately followed by a disjunctive clause that in Hebrew reads almost like but, a leper. Greatness and affliction sit side by side in a single sentence, and that tension, not resolved until the chapter's final scene, is the engine of the whole story.

Against that greatness stands a deliberately small figure, a na'arah qetanah, a young girl, literally a little girl, verse 2, a captive with no status at all. The narrator sets the greatest man in Aram beside the smallest person in his household on purpose, since it is her few words, if only my master would go, that move the entire plot, establishing before a single miracle occurs that greatness of rank has nothing to do with usefulness to God.

When Naaman finally obeys, the verb is rachats, to wash or bathe, the same ordinary verb used for the priestly cleansing rite in Leviticus 14:8-9, where a healed leper must wash his clothes and bathe himself with water before re-entering the camp. Naaman's sevenfold washing in the Jordan is not a magic number invented for this story, it echoes the sevens built into Israel's own law for exactly this kind of cleansing, even though Naaman performs it outside any priest's supervision, in a river rather than a sanctuary.

After he is healed, Naaman offers Elisha what he calls a gift, verse 15, using the word berakah, which more literally means a blessing or a present given out of gratitude. The same word appears when Jacob presses Esau to accept his gift, Genesis 33:11, please accept my blessing, so Naaman instinctively reaches for the very language an earlier patriarch used to try to repay an undeserved kindness, and Elisha's refusal insists that this particular berakah cannot be repaid at all, only received.

Finally, notice how often Naaman now names himself eved, servant, your servant will never again make a burnt offering, may the LORD forgive your servant, please let your servant be given, six times across five verses. A man introduced as a great commander leaves the story calling himself a servant more often than the actual servant, Gehazi, who twice denies being sent anywhere at all, your servant did not go anywhere, even though that is exactly the title and the truth he is trying to escape.

typology.type: A Gentile outsider cleansed through humble, simple obedience rather than status or ritual display
typology.fulfillment: Naaman is healed only once he sets aside rank and expectation to obey a plain word, wash and be clean, prefiguring salvation offered to every nation through simple faith in Christ's word rather than human merit or ceremony, Romans 10:9-13. Jesus cites this healing precisely because it proves God's grace was never confined to ethnic Israel, Luke 4:25-27. The type is not exact, since Naaman's cleansing was physical and temporary, while the cleansing offered in Christ reaches the conscience itself and lasts forever.

typology.type: Washing seven times in the Jordan to be made clean
typology.fulfillment: The sevenfold washing echoes the sevens of Israel's own cleansing law, Leviticus 14:8-9, applied here to a foreigner outside any priestly system. It anticipates the washing of regeneration and the cleansing from sin accomplished through union with Christ, Titus 3:5, 1 Peter 3:21. The type falls short in that water itself did nothing, obedient faith in the prophet's word was the actual means, just as baptism saves not by removing dirt from the body but through the resurrection of Jesus Christ, 1 Peter 3:21.

typology.type: A captive slave girl's few words becoming the means of her captor's salvation
typology.fulfillment: The lowest person in Naaman's household, with no power and no standing, speaks the one sentence that saves her master's life. This anticipates how God chose what is foolish, weak, and lowly in the world's eyes to save those who believe, 1 Corinthians 1:27-29, and how the gospel is first preached by and to the humble and overlooked, Luke 4:18. The correspondence is real but modest, she remains a minor, unnamed figure in the text, a reminder that Scripture does not need to elevate its instruments to use them decisively.

typology.type: Naaman's request for Israelite soil to worship the LORD on foreign ground
typology.fulfillment: Naaman assumes, in an ancient and imperfect way, that worshipping the LORD requires standing on His own land even while living in Aram. Jesus later declares to the woman at the well that true worship will no longer depend on any mountain or any land, but will be in spirit and in truth, John 4:21-24, fulfilling and correcting what Naaman could only reach toward. The type is instructive precisely in its incompleteness, an early, sincere step of faith still bound to categories the gospel would later set free.

study.christ:
This chapter leads to Christ first by contrast in how the unclean are approached. Elisha never leaves his house to meet Naaman, he sends a messenger with instructions and lets a foreign commander stand offended at his own door, verses 9 to 10, keeping the ritual distance Israel's law required around a leper, Leviticus 13:45-46. Jesus does the opposite. When a leper kneels before him, he reaches out his hand and touches the man, Mark 1:41, closing a distance no observant Israelite would have closed, and instead of becoming unclean himself, he makes the unclean man whole. The greater Prophet does not merely command cleansing from a safe distance, he touches what defiles and remains undefiled.

It leads to Christ by confession. Naaman declares there is no God in all the earth except in Israel, verse 15, the furthest a proud Gentile general could travel in a single conversation, and the New Testament later gives believers a confession that completes his, there is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given to mankind by which we must be saved, Acts 4:12. What Naaman discovered about the LORD in general, the church confesses fully in the LORD's own Son.

It leads to Christ by welcome. Naaman is a military enemy of Israel, a man through whom the LORD had actually given Aram victory over God's own people, verse 1, and yet he is the one drawn near, healed, and instructed rather than destroyed. Paul later describes exactly this kind of former enemy, once separate from Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, strangers to the covenants of promise, who have been brought near through the blood of Christ, Ephesians 2:12-13, a nearness Naaman only pictures by carrying two mule loads of foreign soil home with him.

A caution keeps the reading honest. Not every detail here, the number of mules, the specific rivers Naaman names in his complaint, is a coded picture of the gospel. What the chapter supplies is the shape of grace reaching an undeserving outsider through a humbling word, and the New Testament's own explicit use of this account, in Jesus' own mouth, licenses reading it as a genuine, deliberate anticipation of a wider mercy still to come.
study.god:
This chapter opens with a claim easy to miss and startling to consider, that through Naaman the LORD had given victory to Aram, verse 1. Before any Israelite reader meets the healing story, the narrator insists that the God of Israel governs the outcomes of wars fought by Israel's enemies against Israel itself, a sovereignty that refuses to be boxed inside the borders of the covenant people. The LORD who disciplines Israel through Aram's victories is the same LORD who will shortly heal Aram's own celebrated general.

He is also a God who will not be bought. Naaman arrives with a fortune calculated to purchase almost anything, and Elisha, as surely as the LORD lives, before whom I stand, refuses even a fraction of it, verse 16, protecting the truth that this healing was never for sale in the first place. When Gehazi tries privately to collect what his master publicly refused, the LORD's verdict through Elisha shows that grace treated as a commodity brings exactly the judgment grace itself had just removed.

He is patient with a faith still finding its footing. Naaman's requests for soil and for pardon regarding Rimmon are not met with a lecture on consistency but with a simple, gracious release, go in peace, verse 19, showing a God willing to let a new believer work out the practical shape of loyalty to him over time rather than all at once.

And he is a God whose holiness cannot be evaded by rank or nationality. Miriam and Uzziah, both insiders, both once close to God's own house, were struck with this same disease for pride, and now Gehazi joins them, while the outsider who trusted a simple word walks away clean. Status before God has never been a matter of birth, office, or nearness to holy things, but of whether a person will humble himself enough to obey.

Throughout the chapter God works through channels that carry no credit of their own, a nameless captive girl's remark, a river no more impressive to Naaman than two rivers back home, and a plain, unadorned word rather than a display fitting a commander's rank. He does not need an audience worthy of the miracle to perform it, and he does not let the miracle's own witnesses, a king, a commander, a servant, decide for themselves what it is worth.

crossReferences.note: Jesus cites Naaman's healing directly in his hometown synagogue to prove that God's grace in the Old Testament already reached beyond Israel's own borders, a claim so provocative it nearly gets him killed on the spot.

The background law on skin disease and ritual uncleanness frames how serious it is that this chapter names a foreign general's affliction with Israel's own technical term, and later applies the same term to Elisha's own servant.

The priestly rite for a healed leper includes sevenfold sprinkling and washing with water before re-entry into the camp, the same pattern of sevens Naaman performs in the Jordan, though entirely outside priestly supervision.

Miriam is struck leprous, white as snow, the identical description later used of Gehazi, for challenging Moses' unique authority, an earlier instance of this disease falling on a proud insider rather than a humbled outsider.

King Uzziah is struck with leprosy the moment his pride leads him to usurp the priesthood, living cut off from the house of the LORD until his death, another insider judged by the very affliction Naaman is healed of.

Jacob presses Esau to accept his gift, using the same Hebrew word for gift, berakah, that Naaman offers Elisha, so Naaman reaches instinctively for the language an earlier patriarch used to try to repay an undeserved kindness.
Jesus reaches out and touches a leper to heal him, closing a distance Elisha never closes with Naaman, showing the greater Prophet cleansing the unclean by contact rather than by instruction alone.

Jesus heals ten lepers, and the only one who returns to give thanks is a foreigner, a Samaritan, repeating this chapter's pattern that grace is often received most gladly by those furthest from the community that first received God's promises.

Simon the sorcerer's attempt to buy the gift of the Spirit parallels Gehazi's attempt to profit secretly from what God had freely given through Elisha, and both meet a severe rebuke rather than a payout.

Paul describes Gentiles once alienated from the covenants of promise who have been brought near through the blood of Christ, the reality Naaman's healing and his two mule loads of borrowed soil only foreshadow from a great distance.

study.oneStory:
Genesis ends with humanity locked out of the garden, guarded from God's presence by a flaming sword. By the time of this chapter, an enemy commander from a hostile pagan nation is welcomed near enough to be healed, instructed, and sent home in peace, a small but real sign that the door barred in Eden was never going to stay shut to outsiders forever.

The chapter also quietly indicts the very people who should have recognised grace first. Israel's own king despairs rather than trusts, verse 7, and Elisha's own servant, closer to the prophet than anyone else in the story, is the one who is struck with the disease a foreigner has just been healed of. This reversal, insiders failing and an outsider believing, runs all through the rest of Scripture, culminating in Paul's picture of natural branches broken off for unbelief while a wild branch is grafted in by grace, Romans 11:17-24, and warned in the same breath not to grow proud of its own place.

What begins here as a single healing anticipates a much larger project. The prophets already promise a day when the nations will stream to the LORD's mountain, and this chapter is one small, concrete instance of that promise beginning to be kept ahead of schedule, centuries before the gospel is preached to the ends of the earth. It reaches its horizon in a city where the leaves of the tree of life are for the healing of the nations, Revelation 22:2, and where every tribe, tongue, and people once as far from the covenants as Naaman himself stands washed and whole before the throne, Revelation 7:9-14.

Between Eden's closed gate and that open city stands this one Aramean general, kneeling in a river he had mocked only a few verses earlier, discovering that the God he had never worshipped had already decided to make him clean.

sermon.title: The Lepers Are Cleansed
sermon.why: Preached by Timothy J. Keller at Redeemer Presbyterian Church on October 10, 1999, in the series Receiving the Spirit (with Elisha), directly covering 2 Kings 5:1-19, the healing of Naaman.

quiz.q: Who first directed Naaman toward help for his leprosy, and what did she say?

options.text: A captured young Israelite girl serving Naaman's wife, who said the prophet in Samaria could cure him.
options.note: Verses 2 to 3 identify her exact role and words.

options.text: The king of Aram personally recommended Elisha.
options.note: The king only acted after hearing the report from Naaman, who had heard it from the servant girl.

options.text: Naaman's own physicians suggested he travel to Israel.
options.note: No physicians are mentioned; the suggestion came from the captive Israelite girl.

options.text: Elisha sent a personal invitation to Naaman.
options.note: Elisha only responded after hearing of the king of Israel's distress over Naaman's letter; he did not initiate contact.

quiz.q: Why did Naaman initially become enraged at Elisha's instructions?

options.text: He expected a dramatic ritual with the prophet calling on the LORD and waving his hand, and was offended by the simple command to wash in the Jordan.
options.note: Verses 11 to 12 record exactly this expectation and his resulting anger.

options.text: Elisha refused to see him at all.
options.note: Elisha did send him instructions through a messenger; the offense was the simplicity of the command, not a total refusal to engage.

options.text: He was told to pay an enormous sum of money first.
options.note: No payment was demanded before healing; Elisha later refused payment entirely.

options.text: He was told the healing was impossible.
options.note: Elisha's instructions promised healing through washing, not a declaration of impossibility.

quiz.q: What did Naaman confess after he was healed, and how did Elisha respond to his offered gift?

options.text: Naaman confessed there is no God in all the earth except in Israel, and Elisha refused to accept any payment despite being urged.
options.note: Verses 15 to 16 record both his confession and Elisha's firm refusal.

options.text: Naaman confessed his sins but Elisha eagerly accepted his gifts.
options.note: Elisha explicitly and repeatedly refused the gift, even when urged.

options.text: Naaman refused to acknowledge the LORD at all after being healed.
options.note: The text records an explicit, strong confession of the LORD as the only true God.

options.text: Elisha demanded double the payment Naaman had originally offered.
options.note: Elisha refused any payment whatsoever, the opposite of demanding more.

quiz.q: What two requests did Naaman make of Elisha before departing, and how did Elisha respond?

options.text: He asked for Israelite soil to worship the LORD on and pre-emptively asked forgiveness for future required attendance at the temple of Rimmon, and Elisha simply said, go in peace.
options.note: Verses 17 to 19 record both requests and Elisha's brief, gracious dismissal.

options.text: He asked to become an Israelite citizen and to marry an Israelite woman.
options.note: His actual requests concerned soil for worship and a specific moral tension regarding his court duties, not citizenship or marriage.

options.text: He asked Elisha to return with him to Aram permanently.
options.note: No such request is recorded; Naaman intended to return home to serve his own king.

options.text: He asked for nothing further and left immediately without conversation.
options.note: The text records a specific, detailed exchange between Naaman and Elisha before his departure.

quiz.q: What did Gehazi do after Naaman departed, and what was the consequence?

options.text: He secretly pursued Naaman, lied to obtain silver and clothing, then lied to Elisha about it, and as a result Naaman's leprosy came upon him and his descendants forever.
options.note: Verses 20 to 27 record his deception, his lie to Elisha, and the resulting judgment.

options.text: He openly asked Elisha's permission to accept a gift from Naaman.
options.note: Gehazi acted entirely in secret, without Elisha's knowledge or permission, which was central to his sin.

options.text: He refused any payment from Naaman out of respect for Elisha's example.
options.note: Gehazi did precisely the opposite, secretly pursuing payment his master had refused.

options.text: He was rewarded by Elisha for his resourcefulness.
options.note: Elisha pronounced Naaman's own leprosy upon Gehazi as judgment, not a reward.

questions: The captured servant girl, with little power of her own, still spoke a word of hope that changed Naaman's life. Where might God be asking you to speak up in faith even from a position that feels small or powerless?

Naaman nearly walked away from healing because it did not match what he expected from God. Where are you resisting a simple, humbling instruction from God because you wanted something more impressive?
Naaman confessed the LORD alone as God only after humbling himself to obey. What is one area where obedience, not just belief, is the next step God is asking of you?
Elisha refused payment so that grace would remain free and unmistakable. Where might you be tempted to attach strings, price, or personal gain to something God has called you to give freely?

Gehazi's secret greed cost him everything Naaman's public confession had gained. What hidden compromise in your own life needs to be brought into the light before it grows into something far more costly?

translationNotes.note: The BSB footnote clarifies that leper or leprosy in this chapter refers broadly to various skin diseases as categorized in Leviticus 13, not necessarily the specific modern medical condition called leprosy today.
The BSB footnotes convert the gifts Naaman brought to modern equivalents, approximately 754 pounds of silver and 150.8 pounds of gold, underscoring the enormous value he expected to pay for his cure.

Rimmon was a title associated with the Aramean storm god Hadad; Naaman's request for pardon reflects his ongoing court obligation to physically support his king even while attending pagan worship, a tension the text leaves without a direct resolution.
